name: Ambrose of Milan

seo.title: St Ambrose of Milan: the emperor's penance, quotes and feast day
seo.description: Who Ambrose of Milan was, in plain words: made bishop in eight days, Augustine's baptism, the emperor's penance, his words and his feast day.

band.lede: A Roman governor made bishop by a crowd, who baptised Augustine and brought an emperor to public penance.

picture.alt: St Ambrose, grey-bearded in a tall gold mitre and a shimmering blue and gold cope, sits at a table piled with books and turns to look at us, one hand on an open book, a knotted scourge beside his inkwell
picture.credit: Saint Ambrose, Claude Vignon, 1623 or 1625. Minneapolis Institute of Art. Public domain.
picture.creator: Claude Vignon

card.line: A Roman governor made bishop by a crowd, who baptised Augustine and brought an emperor to public penance.

who: Ambrose was the Roman governor at Milan in 374, when the city nearly rioted over its next bishop. He went to the church to keep the peace, and the crowd chose him, though he was not yet baptised. As bishop he preached, wrote hymns and baptised Augustine. He stood up to emperors, and brought one to public penance.

roles.name: Lawyer
roles.line: Pleaded cases at the prefect's court

lines: Made bishop on 7 December 374, still his feast day
Said to have held every office of the Church in between
numbers.src: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 9

lines: After he died, five bishops shared the baptising he had done alone
Even they, says Paulinus, found it hard
numbers.src: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 38

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 339 or 340, probably at **Trier**, in today's Germany. His father, also called Ambrose, then ran the Roman prefecture of Gaul.

facts.label: Grew up
facts.text: At **Rome**, after his father died. His widowed mother raised him with his elder sister Marcellina and his elder brother Satyrus.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **4 April 397**, at Milan, before dawn, after an illness of many days. That night was the vigil of Easter.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In his own basilica at Milan, today **Sant'Ambrogio**, beside the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. The three bodies were found together under the altar in 1864.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Ambrosius**, in Latin. **Sant'Ambrogio**, in Italian. Greek and Russian calendars call him bishop of **Mediolanum**, the old name of Milan.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics and Orthodox, and a Doctor of the Church. Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day too.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: A bishop. His signs are a beehive, a baby in a cradle and a scourge with three knots.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: A great deal: sermons worked up into books on Scripture, a handbook on Christian duty, books on the faith, letters, funeral speeches and hymns.

portrait.alt: A Byzantine miniature on gold: the white-haired, bearded Ambrose in a red cloak and a bishop's stole stands before an arcaded church and a green hill, lifting his veiled hands toward the hand of God in the sky
portrait.credit: Ambrose of Milan, Menologion of Basil II, Constantinople, about 976 to 1025. Vatican Library. Public domain.
portrait.caption: A page from the Menologion of Basil II, a Greek book of saints made in Constantinople between about 976 and 1025. This is his page, for 7 December. Vatican Library. Public domain.

west.text: In the **1916 Roman Martyrology**: the day he died.
**Catholic** memorial, as Bishop and Doctor of the Church. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **OCA** and the **Greek** churches. Also the **Russian Church**, on the old calendar: that is 20 December on today's calendar.

feasts.note: Why 7 December? It is the day he was made bishop, in 374, and East and West keep it alike. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so 7 December falls on 20 December.

traits.title: respectful, but unbending
traits.text: In the struggle over Milan's churches, the court ordered him to leave the city. He told his people he would not run, and he would not fight either. “You yourselves know that I am wont to show respect to our emperors, but not to yield to them, to offer myself freely to punishment, and not to fear what is prepared for me.”

cite.text: Sermon against Auxentius

traits.title: wept with sinners
traits.text: When anyone confessed a sin to him, “he so wept that he compelled that one to weep”. He kept what he heard. The sins confessed to him “he told to no one except to the Lord alone with Whom he pleaded”.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 39

traits.title: gave it away
traits.text: When he became bishop he gave his gold and silver to the church and the poor. In 378 the Goths carried off crowds of captives, and he broke up the church's sacred vessels to buy them back. The Arians blamed him for it. He answered that the Lord Himself would ask why so many were left to die: “It had been better to preserve living vessels than gold ones.”

cite.text: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 2, chapter 28, with its translators' notes; Paulinus, chapter 38

traits.title: busy, and quiet
traits.text: Augustine could seldom get a word with him, for the “crowds of busy people, whose infirmities he devoted himself to”. In his few free moments he read in silence. “His eyes glanced over the pages, and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were silent.” Visitors would sit a while and then leave. “For who dared interrupt one so intent?”

cite.text: Augustine, Confessions, Book 6, chapter 3

traits.title: ate little
traits.text: Paulinus says he wore his body out with fasting. His “habit was never to take breakfast except on the day of Sabbath and the Lord's Day, or when the birthdays of the most celebrated martyrs occurred”. And “he did not shun the work of writing books with his own hand”.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 38

said.lede: Augustine knew him best. Jerome, who mocked his writing, wrote about him while he lived. His secretary Paulinus wrote his *Life* between 412 and 422, at Augustine's request.

quotes.q: To him was I unknowingly led by You, that by him I might knowingly be led to You. That man of God received me like a father, and looked with a benevolent and episcopal kindliness on my change of abode.
quotes.who: Augustine, on coming to Milan in 384

cite.text: Confessions, Book 5, chapter 13

quotes.q: …so that he would often, when he saw me, burst forth into her praises, congratulating me that I had such a mother
quotes.who: Augustine, on how Ambrose spoke of his mother, Monica

cite.text: Confessions, Book 6, chapter 2

quotes.q: I withhold my judgment of him, because he is still alive, fearing either to praise or blame lest in the one event, I should be blamed for adulation, and in the other for speaking the truth.
quotes.who: Jerome, in his book of Christian writers, while Ambrose was alive

cite.text: Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 124

quotes.q: I have learned after great difficulty the differences between an emperor and a priest. It is not easy to find a man capable of teaching me the truth. Ambrosius alone deserves the title of bishop.
quotes.who: The emperor Theodosius, to the bishop of Constantinople, as Theodoret tells it about sixty years later

cite.text: Theodoret, Church History, Book 5, chapter 17

moments.title: The bees
moments.text: The baby lay asleep in his cradle in the courtyard of the governor's house, with his mouth open. A swarm of bees covered his face, going in and out of his mouth. His father stopped the nurse from driving them off. At last they flew up out of sight. His father said, “If this little child shall live he shall be something great.” Paulinus had the family's stories from Ambrose's sister Marcellina.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 1 and 3

moments.title: A bishop's hand
moments.text: After his father died, the family moved to Rome. His sister had vowed herself to virginity, and another consecrated virgin lived with her. The boy saw the women of the house kiss the hands of bishops. So he would hold out his own right hand to this young woman, “because he said that he would be a bishop”. She pushed him away: he was a boy, and did not know what he was saying. Years later he came back to Rome a bishop, and found her still living with his sister. She kissed his hand, and he smiled: “Behold, as I used to tell you, you are kissing the hand of a bishop.”

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 4 and 9

moments.title: Governor
moments.text: He studied law and pleaded cases so well that the prefect Probus made him his adviser. Then he was sent to govern Liguria and Aemilia from Milan. Probus sent him off with words that came true: “Go, act not as judge but as bishop.”

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 5 and 8; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: “Ambrose Bishop!”
moments.text: The Arian bishop Auxentius had died, and Arians and Catholics each wanted a bishop of their own. Ambrose went to the church to keep the peace. As he spoke, “the voice of a child is said to have suddenly cried out among the people”, and the whole crowd took up the cry. He tried everything to put them off. He had people tortured from the judge's seat. He had prostitutes come to his house in public. The crowd only shouted, “Your sin be upon us.” He fled at midnight for Pavia, and in the morning was found at Milan's own Roman Gate. A report went to the emperor. While it was pending, he fled again and hid on the estate of Leontius, a man of rank. When the emperor's answer came, Leontius gave him up. He was baptised, and on the eighth day, 7 December 374, he was made bishop. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* finds the tricks “difficult to believe”.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 6 to 9; Catholic Encyclopedia

moments.title: Augustine
moments.text: A young teacher of rhetoric came from Rome, sent by the city's prefect, Symmachus. He went to hear the famous preacher, at first only to judge his style. Every Sunday he heard him, and he came to see that “all those knots of crafty calumnies, which those deceivers of ours had knit against the divine books, could be unravelled”. Ambrose baptised him at Easter in 387.

cite.text: Augustine, Confessions, Books 5 and 6; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

moments.title: The church he would not hand over
moments.text: The boy emperor Valentinian II and his mother Justina, an Arian, demanded a church in Milan for the Arians. Ambrose refused: “The palaces belong to the Emperor, the churches to the Bishop.” When soldiers ringed the church, his people stayed inside with him. To keep up their spirits he had hymns and psalms sung “after the manner of the Eastern Church”. Augustine's mother Monica was among them. Paulinus says the court's campaign only began to die down after two martyrs were found.

cite.text: Letter 20, to his sister Marcellina; Confessions, Book 9, chapter 7; Paulinus, chapters 13 and 15

moments.title: Two martyrs found
moments.text: He had built a new church, and the people asked him to consecrate it with relics. “Certainly I will if I find any relics of martyrs,” he said. He had the ground dug in front of the chancel screen of Saints Felix and Nabor. “We found two men of marvellous stature, such as those of ancient days.” He names them as the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, long forgotten. As they were carried to his new church, a blind man was healed.

cite.text: Letter 22, to his sister Marcellina

moments.title: The burned synagogue
moments.text: Christians burned a synagogue at Callinicum, a fortified town in the East, “at the instigation of the Bishop”, the report said. The emperor Theodosius ordered that bishop to rebuild it. Ambrose wrote to stop him, then preached at the emperor in church. “You spoke against us today, bishop,” Theodosius said. Ambrose would not go up to the altar until the emperor promised to drop the order. “Go on, with my promise,” said Theodosius.

cite.text: Letter 40, to Theodosius; Paulinus, chapters 22 and 23

moments.title: The emperor's penance
moments.text: After a riot at Thessalonica, the emperor had promised Ambrose to pardon the city. But his officers talked with him in secret, and the city was “given to the sword for almost three hours and many innocent were slain”. Ambrose did not rebuke him in public. He wrote, “I am writing with my own hand that which you alone may read.” He said he dared not offer the sacrifice with the emperor present. Theodosius pleaded that King David had sinned too. The answer came back: “You who have followed him as he sinned, follow him as he corrected himself.” The emperor did public penance.

cite.text: Letter 51, to Theodosius; Paulinus, chapter 24; Britannica

miracles.lede: Paulinus, his secretary, tells many wonders. He says he had them from Ambrose's sister Marcellina, from men who served Ambrose before him, from what he saw himself, and from people who saw Ambrose after his death. He begins with a plea.

pledge.q: I beseech you all, in whose hands this book will fall, to believe that what we say is true.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 2

feature.title: accounts of one blind man healed

items.title: Ambrose
items.text: He wrote to his sister about the finding of the martyrs. A blind man was healed as the bodies were carried to the new church. In a sermon he named the man, “Severus, a butcher by trade”. Severus could call as witnesses the people who had supported him while he was blind.
items.quote: He declares that when he touched the hem of the robe of the martyrs, wherewith the sacred relics were covered, his sight was restored.
items.witness: Ambrose was there. It was his own procession.

cite.text: Letter 22, to his sister Marcellina

items.title: Augustine
items.text: Augustine was living in Milan, not yet baptised. The man had been blind many years and was well known in the city. He heard why the crowd was cheering and asked to be led there. He touched the bier with his handkerchief and put it to his eyes, and they were opened.
items.quote: The miracle which was wrought at Milan when I was there, and by which a blind man was restored to sight
items.witness: Augustine adds that the emperor was in the city, and “the occurrence was witnessed by an immense concourse of people”.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 9, chapter 7; City of God, Book 22, chapter 8

items.title: Paulinus
items.text: Paulinus names the man too. He says Severus touched the martyrs' clothing and saw at once. When Paulinus wrote, Severus was still serving in the same church.
items.quote: Even a blind man, Severus by name, who to the present day devoutly serves in that same basilica which is called the Ambrosian … immediately received his sight.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 14

note.text: Augustine says the news of it held back the empress's campaign against Ambrose. Her mind was “restrained from the fury of persecuting”.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 9, chapter 7

more.title: The paralysed woman at Rome
more.text: At a noble lady's house across the Tiber, Ambrose had come to offer the Holy Sacrifice. A woman who kept the baths lay paralysed. She had herself carried there, and touched his clothes as he prayed and laid his hands on her. Then she kissed them. Paulinus heard it in Rome years later, “on the authority of holy men”.
more.quote: her health was restored immediately and she began to walk

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 10

more.title: A boy raised at Florence
more.text: At Florence, Ambrose stayed in the house of Decens. The little son of the house, Pansophius, fell ill and died. His mother laid the body on Ambrose's bed while he was out. When he came back, he lay down on the child, as Elisha did, and prayed. Paulinus notes that Ambrose never mentioned it in his writings. He names the boy's mother, Pansophia, as his source for another story from Florence.
more.quote: he laid himself down on the body of the child and through prayer succeeded in returning alive to the mother the child, whom he had found dead

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 28 and 50

more.title: Fire on his head
more.text: A few days before his last illness, Ambrose was dictating a commentary on Psalm 44 (43 in his Latin Bible), and Paulinus was taking it down. Paulinus saw this himself, and was so struck that he could not write. Ambrose stopped dictating that day, and he could not finish that psalm.
more.quote: suddenly a fire in the shape of a small shield covered his head, and gradually it entered through his mouth like a householder into his home, after which his face became like snow

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 42

more.title: The angel at his ear
more.text: A sharp Arian debater sat in church while Ambrose preached. He later said he saw an angel speaking into the bishop's ear, as if Ambrose were passing on the angel's words. He changed sides, and began to defend the faith he used to attack.
more.quote: saw, as he himself afterwards said, an angel speaking into the ears of the bishop as he preached

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 17

more.title: Nicentius's feet
more.text: Nicentius, a retired tribune, had such pain in his feet that he was rarely seen in public. At the altar, Ambrose stepped on his foot by accident, and he cried out. Then he heard Ambrose speak. His feet never troubled him again, and he told of it with tears when Ambrose died.
more.quote: Go, and henceforth you will be well.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 44

more.title: A warning at Sirmium
more.text: At Sirmium the empress Justina's party tried to drive Ambrose out of the church. An Arian girl climbed onto the platform and seized his robe, to drag him off to be beaten. He told her it did not become her “to lay hands on any bishop”, and that she should fear the judgment of God. Paulinus tells two more stories of men who spoke against Ambrose after his death and died suddenly.
more.quote: on the following day he conducted her dead to the grave repaying kindness for insult

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapters 11 and 54

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: The Arians at court said the cures at the martyrs' tomb were staged. Paulinus reports their charge, that Ambrose “by means of money had procured men to say falsely that they were troubled by unclean spirits”. Ambrose answered them about the blind man: “They deny that the blind man received sight, but he denies not that he is healed.” A later judgement is about Paulinus's book as history. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1907 calls it “extremely disappointing”.

cites.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 15

words.note: Ambrose wrote a great deal, mostly sermons worked up into books. These lines are from his books and letters, in the translation of 1896 by H. de Romestin and others, and from *On Naboth*, translated by Martin McGuire in 1927.

feature.q: For the Emperor is within the Church, not above it.
feature.ctx: Preached while soldiers ringed the church the court wanted for the Arians. In Latin, {la|Imperator enim intra Ecclesiam, non supra Ecclesiam est.} It goes on: “For a good emperor seeks the aid of the Church and does not refuse it.”

cite.text: Sermon against Auxentius

quotes.q: I shall be able to grieve, to weep, to groan; against weapons, soldiers, Goths, my tears are my weapons, for these are a priest's defense.
quotes.who: To his people, shut in the church with him.

cite.text: Sermon against Auxentius

quotes.q: They declare also that the people have been led astray by the strains of my hymns. I certainly do not deny it.
quotes.who: On the hymns he taught his people to sing.

cite.text: Sermon against Auxentius

quotes.q: Not from your own do you bestow upon the poor man, but you make return from what is his. For what has been given as common for the use of all, you appropriate to yourself alone. The earth belongs to all, not to the rich.

cite.text: On Naboth, chapter 12

quotes.q: You cover your walls, you strip men naked. … The poor man seeks money and has it not; a man asks for bread, and your horse champs gold under his teeth.
quotes.who: To a rich man, proud of his house.

cite.text: On Naboth, chapter 13

quotes.q: The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out, and to spend on those who need.
quotes.who: On breaking up the church's plate to free captives.

cite.text: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 2, chapter 28

quotes.q: Beasts do not drive out beasts, yet man shuts out man.
quotes.who: Against driving strangers out of a city in a famine, as Rome had done.

cite.text: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 3, chapter 7

quotes.q: Now no one can repent to good purpose unless he hopes for mercy.
quotes.who: Against the Novatians, who would not pardon grave sinners.

cite.text: Concerning Repentance, Book 1, chapter 1

quotes.q: So it happened that I began to teach before I began to learn.
quotes.who: On being taken from the judge's seat to be made bishop.

cite.text: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 1

extras.title: What he is criticised for
extras.lede: Some of what he did draws sharp criticism. Here it is, in his own words and in his critics'.

items.title: The synagogue at Callinicum
items.text: His letter to the emperor called the burned synagogue “a home of unbelief, a house of impiety, a receptacle of folly, which God Himself has condemned”. He offered to take the blame in the local bishop's place. Paulinus tells the story as a win for the Church. The historian Peter Brown, writing in *Britannica*, sees in his clashes with the court “a sinister vein of demagoguery”.
items.quote: I declare that I set fire to the synagogue, or at least that I ordered those who did it, that there might not be a place where Christ was denied.

cite.text: Letter 40, to Theodosius; Paulinus, chapters 22 and 23; Britannica

items.title: The Altar of Victory
items.text: In 384 pagan senators, led by Symmachus, asked for the Altar of Victory to go back in the Senate, and for their rites to be paid for again. Ambrose argued against it, and won. In his view no pagan was being forced. *Britannica* puts it the other way: “In 384 he secured the rejection of an appeal for tolerance by pagan members of the Roman senate”.
items.quote: No one is injured because God is set before him. He keeps his own opinion. You do not compel a man against his will to worship what he dislikes.

cite.text: Letter 17, to Valentinian II; Britannica

items.title: Daughters against their parents
items.text: He urged young women to vow themselves to virginity, even when their parents begged them not to. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says “many a mother refused to permit her daughters to listen to his words”. He even had to answer the charge that he was emptying the empire of people.
items.quote: Conquer your affection first, O maiden. If you conquer your home, you conquer the world.

cite.text: Concerning Virgins, Book 1, chapter 12; Catholic Encyclopedia

items.title: Borrowed from the Greeks
items.text: He drew heavily on Greek writers, “especially St. Basil the Great and Didymus of Alexandria, from whom no less a man than St. Jerome accused him of plagiarizing”, as his translators of 1896 put it. Without naming him, Jerome called his book on the Holy Spirit “flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty”. Rufinus took Ambrose's side: “You observe how he treats Ambrose.”
items.quote: I read some time ago the treatise of a certain person on the Holy Spirit, and I recognized then, according to the sentence of Terence, bad things in Latin taken from good things in Greek.

cite.text: Jerome, as quoted by Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2

myths.claim: He and Augustine made up the *Te Deum* together, singing verse by verse, on the night of Augustine's baptism.
myths.truth: A legend first found about four hundred years later. “This tradition is now generally rejected by scholars.” Some old manuscripts name Nicetas, bishop of Remesiana, instead. Some church *Lives* still credit him with it.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Te Deum; OCA; azbyka.ru

myths.claim: *When in Rome, do as the Romans do* is his saying.
myths.truth: His real advice, as Augustine reports it, was about fasting on Saturdays: “When I visit Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast.” The proverb in its familiar words is not his.

cite.text: Augustine, Letter 54, to Januarius

myths.claim: He met the emperor at the church door, stopped him, and turned him away with a long speech.
myths.truth: That scene and its speeches are Theodoret's, written about sixty years later. Ambrose's own account is a private letter. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* says the story “is shown by modern criticism to have been greatly exaggerated”.

cite.text: Theodoret, Church History, Book 5, chapter 17; Letter 51; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.truth: So says the *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1907. But Paulinus says he died in the hour before daybreak, and that his body lay in the great church “the same night in which we kept the vigil of Easter”. That makes it the Saturday before Easter.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 48; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.truth: “Ambrosian” came to mean a style of hymn, not an author. Four are accepted by all as his. Augustine quotes three of them and names Ambrose as their author.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Ambrosian Hymnography

myths.claim: He wrote the commentary on Paul's letters that was printed with his works.
myths.truth: Its author is unknown, and scholars call him Ambrosiaster. Erasmus first doubted it was Ambrose's, in the 1500s.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia, Ambrosiaster

stood.lede: Every line shown is his own. Two come to us through others: Augustine quotes the line on effort, and the Catena Aurea, a collection of the Fathers made by Thomas Aquinas, keeps the line on riches.

rich.work: Exposition of the Gospel of Luke, Book 8, as the Catena Aurea gives it

body.work: Letter 63, to the Church at Vercelli

rulers.work: Letter 17, to the Emperor Valentinian II

effort.work: On Flight from the World, as Augustine quotes it in On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 20

circle.name: Augustine of Hippo
circle.text: He came to Milan to teach rhetoric, and went to hear Ambrose at first only for the style. Ambrose baptised him at Easter in 387. Years later Augustine asked Paulinus to write Ambrose's *Life*.

cite.text: Confessions, Books 5 and 6; Paulinus, chapter 1

circle.name: Monica
circle.text: Augustine's mother. She followed her son to Milan, and “she loved that man as an angel of God”. When he banned the African custom of bringing food and wine to the martyrs' shrines, she gave it up at once.

cite.text: Confessions, Book 6, chapters 1 and 2

circle.name: Marcellina
circle.text: His elder sister, about ten years older, a consecrated virgin. She helped their widowed mother raise the boys. Paulinus had many of his stories from her.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia; Paulinus, chapter 1

circle.name: Satyrus
circle.text: His elder brother. When Ambrose was made bishop, Satyrus gave up his own post to run his affairs. When Satyrus died, about 378, Ambrose preached two funeral speeches for him.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia; On the Death of Satyrus

circle.name: Theodosius I
circle.text: The emperor he faced over Callinicum and over Thessalonica. Theodosius died at Milan in 395, “with Ambrose at his bedside and the name of Ambrose on his lips”, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. Ambrose preached at his funeral.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia; Britannica

circle.name: Symmachus
circle.text: Prefect of Rome and a leading pagan. In 384 he asked for the Altar of Victory back, and Ambrose defeated him. That same year Symmachus sent the young Augustine to teach at Milan.

cite.text: Letters 17 and 18; Confessions, Book 5, chapter 13

circle.name: Jerome
circle.text: No friend. While Ambrose lived, Jerome would not judge him in his book of Christian writers. Elsewhere he mocked his book on the Holy Spirit. Rufinus says he called Ambrose a jackdaw dressed in other birds' feathers.

cite.text: Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 124; Rufinus, Apology, Book 2

circle.name: Martin of Tours
circle.text: Both men stood up to the usurper Maximus at Trier. Ambrose would not share communion with the bishops “who sought the death of any one, even though they were heretics”, and was sent away. Martin begged Maximus to spare the followers of Priscillian.

cite.text: Letter 24; Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, Book 2

circle.name: Simplicianus
circle.text: The next bishop of Milan, and an old man. As Ambrose lay dying, four deacons at the far end of the portico whispered about who should follow him. When they named Simplicianus, Ambrose called out three times, “Old but good.” The deacons fled in fright.

cite.text: Paulinus, chapter 46

death.big: He died at Milan before dawn on 4 April 397. That same night the church kept the vigil of Easter.
paras: He had said he would be with them until Easter. He fell ill after ordaining a bishop for Pavia, and lay in bed for many days. Count Stilicho feared that Italy would be ruined without him. He sent Milan's leading men to beg Ambrose to pray for a longer life.
From late afternoon until he died, he prayed with his arms stretched out in the form of a cross. “We indeed saw his lips move but his voice we did not hear.”

Honoratus, bishop of Vercelli, was resting upstairs. He heard a voice call him three times: “Arise, hasten, because now he is about to depart.” He came down and gave Ambrose the Body of the Lord, and “when he took and swallowed it he breathed forth his spirit”.
On Easter morning his body was carried to his basilica, with Jews and pagans among the mourners. He was buried beside the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, as he had wished.

later.title: Seen that night
later.text: Paulinus adds that “many baptized infants as they were coming from the font saw him”, some on his throne and some walking, though their parents could not. Others said they saw a star over his body. At the funeral next morning, crowds threw handkerchiefs and belts, so that they might touch the body.

items.q: I have not so lived among you that I am ashamed to live nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord!

prayer.intro: He had been rushed from the judge's seat to the bishop's chair. In his book on repentance, he prays about it.
prayer.q: Preserve, O Lord, Thy work, guard the gift which Thou hast given even to him who shrank from it. For I knew that I was not worthy to be called a bishop, because I had devoted myself to this world, but by Thy grace I am what I am. And I am indeed the least of all bishops, and the lowest in merit; yet since I too have undertaken some labour for Thy holy Church, watch over this fruit, and let not him whom when lost Thou didst call to the priesthood, to be lost when a priest. And first grant that I may know how with inmost affection to mourn with those who sin … Grant that so often as the sin of any one who has fallen is made known to me I may suffer with him, and not chide him proudly, but mourn and weep, so that weeping over another I may mourn for myself.

tidbits.text: When his mother Monica died, Augustine held back his tears all day. Then he slept, and woke with Ambrose's hymn {la|Deus Creator omnium} in his mind. It praises God for sleep, which eases anxious grief. At last he let himself weep.

cite.text: Augustine, Confessions, Book 9, chapter 12

tidbits.text: Frigitil, a queen of the Marcomanni, heard of him and believed. She asked him to write out the faith for her. He did, and urged her to keep her husband at peace with Rome. She hurried to Milan to meet him, but he had died.

cite.text: Paulinus, Life of St Ambrose, chapter 36

tidbits.text: His handbook for his clergy, On the Duties, takes its title and plan from Cicero's book On Duties. Cicero wrote his for his son. Ambrose wrote his, he says, for his children in the Gospel.

cite.text: On the Duties of the Clergy, Book 1, chapter 7, and its translators' introduction

tidbits.text: His hymns are built of short verses: four lines of eight syllables, easy to learn and sing. For centuries, almost every hymn in Latin worship kept that shape.
